name: Gluten-free for skin
lead: Gluten-free for skin means cutting out gluten-containing grains such as wheat, barley and rye in the hope of clearer, calmer, less inflamed skin. People who try it tend to be aiming at fewer breakouts, less redness and a smoother complexion, and some lifters report that cutting back on wheat made their skin look better.[1][2]

A gluten-free diet is the established treatment for celiac disease, and Wikipedia reports it as the treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis, a celiac-related skin condition; non-coeliac gluten sensitivity may include eczema or rash.[1] It has also been a popular fad diet since the early 2000s.[1]
Dermatology reviews on diet and acne describe glycemic index, dairy, fats and probiotics as the factors studied, and do not highlight gluten.[3]

angle.text: Followers say avoiding gluten calms inflammation and reduces breakouts or redness, giving a smoother complexion. The clearest skin link is in people with celiac-related rashes, where the diet is the treatment.

infobox: Celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, wheat allergy [1]

paras: For celiac disease the diet is lifelong.[1] Wheat allergy can cause rashes or hyperpigmentation, and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity is diagnosed after celiac disease and wheat allergy are excluded.[1] Dermatitis herpetiformis is treated with a gluten-free diet.[1]

A 2021 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology reports that low-glycemic diets are linked to fewer acne lesions, milk is associated with more acne, and omega-3 and gamma-linolenic acids are associated with fewer lesions, with studies limited in quality.[3] Gluten is not among the factors in the portion of the review examined.[3]

No studies found of gluten-free diets for acne in people without celiac disease. Studies of non-coeliac gluten sensitivity are mixed: a 2013 placebo-controlled trial found no difference between gluten and placebo, a 2015 trial found gluten triggered symptoms, and a 2018 study suggested fructans may be responsible.[1]

sections.h: Use in lifting and bodybuilding communities
paras: A T Nation poster who cut about 85 percent of their wheat intake reported more energy in the mornings and thought their skin was smoother.[2] The thread was about the book Wheat Belly.
Wikipedia notes nutritional gaps, cross-contamination and the recommendation to see a physician before going gluten-free so celiac disease can be tested accurately.[1]

timeline.event: FDA issues its final rule on gluten-free labeling.[1]
American Journal of Clinical Dermatology review of diet and acne published.[3]

lore.intro: In strength-training forums gluten and wheat are sometimes discussed as a cause of puffiness or skin issues.[2]

claims.claim: Cutting wheat or gluten makes skin smoother
claims.believers: A T Nation poster who reduced wheat said they had more energy and believed their skin was smoother.[2]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews of diet and acne focus on glycemic load, dairy, fats and probiotics; no trial of gluten-free diets for acne was found.[3]

claims.claim: A gluten-free diet clears rash in celiac-related skin disease
claims.believers: Wikipedia reports that the gluten-free diet is the treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the gluten-free diet as the established treatment for celiac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis.[1]

card.summary: Going gluten-free for skin: essential for celiac-linked rashes, but no acne trials were found.
card.note: Gluten-free substitutes can lack iron and B vitamins and add sugar and fat.

quick.overview:
Gluten-free for skin is the idea that avoiding wheat, barley and rye clears acne or reduces inflammation. It circulates widely in wellness and looksmaxxing spaces.

A gluten-free diet is the established treatment for celiac disease and for dermatitis herpetiformis. Wikipedia's acne article does not discuss gluten, and no acne-specific trials were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Believers point to gluten-driven inflammation. In medical contexts, a gluten-free diet works for autoimmune gluten-triggered conditions such as celiac disease and the skin rash dermatitis herpetiformis.
quick.risks: Poorly chosen replacements can cause nutritional gaps such as lower iron and B vitamins and more sugar and saturated fat. Clinicians advise testing for celiac disease before starting the diet.
